summary.text: Early forms of 元 are interpreted as a human figure with a mark at the head. The graph is associated with ‘head’; inscriptions also use it for ‘first’ and ‘beginning.’ Its familiar strokes do not establish a split into 儿 and 二.

formation.text: Pictographic: the early graph is interpreted as a human figure whose head is marked by a point or square, sometimes reduced to a horizontal stroke. This describes the whole pictorial form; the dossier does not establish distinct internal components. The received Shuowen analysis, ‘beginning; from 一 and 兀,’ is a later interpretation. Later readers disagreed whether 兀 was phonetic or contributed the head sense; another proposal reads the upper strokes as 上 over 人, but that reading is challenged by early point-marked forms.

history.text: The curated image is a modern redraw in a Shuowen seal-script style, not an ancient artifact or a depiction of the earliest head-marked forms. Paleographic accounts list oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript, seal-script, and Qin-slip examples, but their glyph images were not inspected here, so no stroke-by-stroke sequence is asserted.

The proposal that 元 and 兀 split from one graph is reported in the dossier, but it is not established as the origin of 元. The transmitted Shuowen breakdown and later disagreement about 兀 likewise do not independently prove the graph’s original construction.

uncertainties.text: The early graph’s head-marked pictorial interpretation is supported, but the exact identification of its strokes as a person 儿 plus 二 is not established. The alternative 上-over-人 analysis is reported and challenged; neither should be treated as a settled decomposition.

The meanings ‘head,’ ‘first/beginning,’ and ‘great’ are supported in different contexts, but the dossier does not document the exact semantic path among them. The underlying ancient pronunciation of the depicted object is also not established, so no sound-component analysis follows from character-level readings.

The cited oracle-bone and bronze examples are identified by period and context, without exact dates established here. The transmitted Zuo zhuan and Mengzi quotations attest textual uses but are not dated manuscript witnesses.

senses.text: Early forms are interpreted as picturing a human head, but the cited oracle-bone and bronze examples use 元 for other meanings; ‘head’ is attested in transmitted Zuo zhuan and Mengzi passages.

senses.period: oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze contexts; exact dates unresolved
senses.text: The oracle-bone example 元卜 is interpreted as ‘first divination.’ Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use 元 in 元年, ‘first year.’ These examples support early ‘first/beginning’ use, without establishing that it predates every other sense.

senses.period: bronze inscriptional use; exact date unresolved
senses.text: The bronze phrase 元德 is interpreted as ‘great virtue.’ The dossier does not establish whether this use developed from ‘head’ or ‘first/beginning.’

developments.text: A development from ‘head’ to ‘first/beginning’ is proposed, but the evidence here gives no dated sequence demonstrating that transition.

limitations.text: The early pictorial interpretation identifies a proposed referent, not a securely documented original spoken meaning. The dossier does not establish a complete chronology among ‘head,’ ‘first/beginning,’ and ‘great.’
Other current glosses, including ‘origin’ and ‘dollar,’ appear in metadata, but this dossier supplies no historical attestations or development account for them.

overview.text: 元 is linked to ‘head’ through an early picture of a person with the head marked. In inscriptions it also means ‘first’ or ‘beginning’; how those meanings connect is uncertain.
